extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, publishers, and stakeholders interested in peer review practices
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive standards for implementing or evaluating open peer review (forms such as open identities, open reports, and open participation) across journals, preprint platforms, and publishing services. Covers definitions, historical implementations, platform choices, and observed advantages/disadvantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors and reviewers are aware of each other's identity; may or may not be disclosed to the public. Defined as 'any scholarly review mechanism providing disclosure of author and referee identities to one another at any point during the peer review or publication process'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with traditional single-blind (authors' names disclosed to reviewers) and double-blind (authors' and reviewers' names anonymous except to editors). Observed effects: argued to make reviewers more tactful and constructive, help detect conflicts of interest, but may increase reviewer decline rates and allow accumulation of adversaries. Trials (e.g., BMJ) did not find significant effects on review quality or acceptance rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Making the reviewers' reports public, instead of disclosing them only to the article's authors; may include publishing authors' replies and editors' recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often applies to accepted articles (not always to rejected ones). Examples: BMJ/BMC pre-publication histories, Life, and Nature trials. Studies show mixed impacts on review quality and reviewer behavior; some journals publish signed review reports alongside accepted papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowing self-selected reviewers (the wider community) to comment on an article, rather than (or in addition to) having reviewers selected by editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assumes the article text is openly accessible. Self-selected reviewers may be screened or unscreened, and may contribute short comments or full reviews. Criticisms include potential for popularity contests favoring well-known authors; proponents argue it can broaden voices, train early-career researchers, and increase review quantity and diversity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of pre-publication history / review history
rubrics_metrics.description: Posting the entire pre-publication history of the article online, including signed reviews, previous versions, names of handling editors, and author responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by journals/publishers such as BMJ, BioMed Central, Semantic Web journal, and eLife (plans). Can increase transparency and enable external scrutiny; some venues publish reviews even for rejected submissions (Semantic Web).

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-publication peer review and versioned articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing articles before peer review and then publishing invited peer review reports (and reviewer names) with the article as they arrive, linking author-revised versions to the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implemented by F1000Research and ScienceOpen; supports rapid dissemination followed by transparent review and versioning. Enables readers to see review timeline and revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open peer review of preprints
rubrics_metrics.description: Facilitating open peer review on preprint servers or via platforms that host reviews alongside preprints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platforms and examples: OpenReview (flexible access controls), PREreview (empowering diverse researchers), bioRxiv (allow posting reviews), Outbreak Science Rapid PREreview (COVID-19 rapid reviews), Qeios. Common in computer science conferences and preprint ecosystems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and scope of identity disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions about when identities are revealed (during review, after acceptance, only to authors, or publicly) and to whom the identities are disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different implementations affect reviewer willingness to review and candor. Nature's experiments and BMJ trials examined effects; knowledge of simultaneous anonymous review may reduce uptake of open trials. Policies vary across publishers (some reveal reviewers to authors only; others publish reviewer names with reports).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer selection model (editorial vs author-solicited vs community)
rubrics_metrics.description: Who selects reviewers: editors invite reviewers, authors solicit reviewers (e.g., Biology Direct model), or self-selected community reviewers contribute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biology Direct: authors must find three Editorial Board members to review; reviewers cannot suppress publication. Trade-offs include speed, impartiality, and potential biases depending on selection mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer gatekeeping power (ability to suppress publication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether reviewers can prevent publication or whether publication proceeds regardless of review recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models like Philica and Biology Direct limit reviewer gatekeeping (reviewers cannot suppress publication), while traditional models give reviewers veto power. This affects editorial control, author autonomy, and responsibility for quality control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Screening and credentialing of open participants
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether self-selected or crowd reviewers are screened for credentials or allowed to contribute without formal vetting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open participation implementations vary: some screen contributors for basic credentials, others are open to anyone. Screening affects review quality and inclusivity; platforms like PREreview aim to empower historically excluded researchers while providing training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement or encouragement of sharing raw data during review
rubrics_metrics.description: Asking or requiring authors to share raw data as part of the peer review process to address reproducibility concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Has been controversial historically; some journals now require access to raw data for peer review. Examples include calls for open data after high-profile retractions (e.g., COVID-19 related cases). Low compliance in prior requests has been observed in some fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform and access-control choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Choices about the technical platform and the configurable options for who sees what information and when (e.g., OpenReview's flexible system).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platforms differ in features: versioning, access controls, public comment interfaces, and linkage between reviews and articles. These technical choices enable different flavors of open peer review familiar in computer science conferences, F1000Research, ScienceOpen, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowd or closed crowd collaborative review
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a pool (open or closed) of expert reviewers who collaboratively comment on manuscripts (e.g., Synlett's closed crowd peer review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models vary from fully open crowd reviewing to curated closed expert pools; collaborative commenting can produce richer, community-driven feedback but requires coordination and curation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and evaluative outcomes as metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluative measures related to openness: transparency, honesty of reviews, incentives, ability to detect conflicts of interest, reviewer tactfulness, and changes in reviewer behavior or acceptance rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments for openness include increased honesty, better detection of editorial conflicts, and fostering collaboration; observed downsides include higher reviewer decline rates and concerns about declines in criticism. Empirical studies show mixed results on effects on quality; open reports enable quantitative studies of peer review (e.g., correlation of review scrutiny with paper impact).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms to judge review quality and justifiability
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly assessing the accuracy, justifiability, or quality of peer reviews themselves (e.g., Peerage of Science judged and scored peer reviews).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some services implemented scoring/judging of reviews to incentivize good reviewing; such mechanisms can be used to allocate reviews to journals or to provide reputational incentives for reviewers.
